summary:
Thermodynamic Pulse is a data-driven research project investigating how ocean temperatures and atmospheric conditions influence the environment in which tropical cyclones intensify over the Bay of Bengal.

The project analyses historical ocean–atmosphere observations from 2002–2025 using NASA datasets accessed through Giovanni, including MODIS Aqua, MERRA-2, AIRS, Aquarius and GPM. It examines sea-surface temperature, surface pressure, wind speed, humidity, outgoing longwave radiation and salinity using data processing, statistical analysis and linear regression.

We also compare preliminary 2026 daytime sea-surface temperatures across three locations: Northern Bay (28.01°C), Central Bay (29.23°C) and Offshore Andhra (29.11°C).

Our interactive platform features four sections: Overview, Statistical Analysis, Three-Clue Forensics and Floating Bob Simulator. We additionally propose BOB Ocean Beacon, a conceptual buoy-monitoring system designed to collect supplementary ocean and atmospheric observations.

Built using Python and Streamlit, Thermodynamic Pulse combines scientific data analysis with interactive visualisation to make complex ocean conditions easier to understand.

Our goal is to encourage better ocean monitoring and research into cyclone intensification. The project does not claim to predict cyclones or establish formal marine heatwave events from the available data.
details:
Thermodynamic Pulse: Decadal & Pre-Cyclone Marine Heatwave Forensics in the Bay of Bengal

Thermodynamic Pulse is a data-driven ocean and atmospheric research project that investigates how changing ocean conditions and atmospheric signals shape the environment in which tropical cyclones can intensify over the Bay of Bengal.

Our project combines historical observations from 2002–2025 with focused 2026 sea-surface temperature comparisons at three locations: the Northern Bay, Central Bay, and Offshore Andhra. Using NASA Earth-observation and atmospheric datasets, we examine variables such as sea-surface temperature, surface pressure, wind speed, relative humidity, outgoing longwave radiation, and sea-surface salinity.

How does it work?

The project processes historical datasets obtained through NASA Giovanni. We clean and organise the data, remove invalid values, calculate annual averages, and apply linear regression to examine long-term trends. We also compare preliminary 2026 sea-surface temperature observations across the three selected locations.

Our interactive platform presents this research through four sections: Overview, Statistical Analysis, Three-Clue Forensics, and Floating Bob Simulator. Together, these sections help users explore the data, understand the relationship between ocean and atmospheric conditions, and learn why multiple environmental factors matter when studying cyclone intensification.

An important part of our research is understanding the connection between warm ocean water, upper-ocean heat, salinity, stratification, and air–sea energy exchange. We also consider atmospheric factors such as wind shear and humidity. Rather than assuming that warm sea-surface temperatures automatically cause stronger cyclones, we investigate the combination of conditions that can create a favourable environment.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project aims to make ocean–atmosphere information easier to explore and understand. By bringing different environmental indicators together, it provides a starting point for studying marine heatwave conditions and their possible relevance to cyclone development.

It also highlights the importance of collecting more detailed ocean observations, particularly in coastal and offshore regions of the Bay of Bengal. Our proposed BOB (Bay of Bengal) Ocean Beacon concept explores how supplementary monitoring could contribute to future research.

Tools and Technologies

We used Python for data processing and analysis, alongside Pandas for handling datasets, statistical methods and linear regression for trend analysis, and visualisation tools to communicate findings through an interactive web platform. The project also uses NASA Giovanni data exports and a web-based Floating Bob Simulator to demonstrate our proposed monitoring concept.

The proposed BOB Ocean Beacon is designed around sensors for sea-surface temperature, salinity, wind speed and direction, atmospheric pressure, GPS, data logging, telemetry, and solar-powered operation. It is a conceptual design and has not yet been physically deployed.

Creativity and Team Considerations

The creative aspect of Thermodynamic Pulse is its combination of historical climate analysis, focused regional observations, interactive scientific communication, and a practical ocean-monitoring proposal within one project.

We considered geographical differences across the Bay of Bengal, the availability and resolution of satellite datasets, the physical relationship between ocean and atmospheric conditions, the importance of reliable measurements, and the limitations of the available observations.

We also prioritised scientific accuracy. Our available eight-day and monthly observations cannot independently establish formal marine heatwave events, which require daily SST measurements and a seasonally varying climatological threshold. Similarly, our analysis does not claim to predict cyclones or establish that a particular marine heatwave caused a cyclone to intensify.

Ultimately, Thermodynamic Pulse aims to connect ocean observations with meaningful scientific understanding and encourage better monitoring of the Bay of Bengal. It moves beyond simply displaying temperature values to exploring the broader ocean–atmosphere environment and the observations needed for more detailed future research.
